title: The adjoint method gets the gradient of a loss through an ODE solve by integrating one more ODE backwards, and a finite-difference check proves it right
summary: To train a neural ODE you need the derivative of a loss with respect to the weights through the solver. The adjoint method gets it from a second ODE integrated backwards in time, with a memory cost that does not grow with the number of steps. Whatever way the gradient is obtained, it must be checked against central finite differences, whose error first falls and then rises with the step because of truncation and rounding.

The dashed tolerance line and the marker where it was crossed: the stopping criterion actually met.
Parameters flat near the end: converged. Parameters running into a bound: the problem is constrained by the bound, not by the data.
The vertical line at the maximum iteration: the budget, not the solution, ended a run that never crosses the tolerance.
read_the_figure.proves: A run that crossed the tolerance with parameters inside their bounds has converged for that objective; a gradient method also needs its gradient verified separately.

terms.meaning: A scalar that depends on the weights only through the ODE solution at one or several times.
The sensitivity of the loss to the state at time t, obtained by integrating backwards from the final time.
The linear ODE that a(t) satisfies, driven by the transposed Jacobian of the right-hand side.
Differentiate the solver's steps one by one; exact for the discrete scheme but stores every step.
Approximate a derivative with function values on both sides of the point; error falls as the step squared.
The two parts of the finite-difference error: one shrinks with the step, the other grows like machine precision over the step.
Compare an analytic or adjoint gradient with a finite-difference value and report the relative error.

remember: For $\dot y=f(y,\theta)$ and $L=\ell(y(T))$: $\dot a=-(\partial f/\partial y)^{\top}a$, $a(T)=\partial\ell/\partial y(T)$, and $dL/d\theta=\int_0^Ta^{\top}\,\partial f/\partial\theta\,dt$.
The adjoint costs about one more solve, in dimension $2d+p$ when the parameter integral is carried along, and needs no stored activations.
The adjoint solve needs $y(t)$ backwards in time: it is recomputed by integrating back, which is unstable for dissipative or stiff problems; checkpointing is the remedy.
Central difference error is $\approx\tfrac16 L'''\eta^2+\epsilon_{\text{mach}}|L|/\eta$, minimised near $\eta\sim\epsilon_{\text{mach}}^{1/3}\approx6\times10^{-6}$ in double precision.
A gradient that passes at relative error $10^{-6}$ or better in double precision is considered correct.

understand.title: Easy: ask how the end result depends on every instant
understand.text: The loss only looks at the end state. The adjoint is a number attached to each moment, saying how much a small push on the state at that moment would change the loss. It is found by starting at the end, where the answer is known, and walking back to the start, collecting how the weights acted on the way.

understand.title: Medium: where the equation comes from
understand.text: Add the constraint with a multiplier: $\mathcal L=\ell(y(T))-\int_0^Ta^{\top}(\dot y-f)\,dt$. Integrating by parts and requiring the terms with $\delta y$ to cancel gives the backward equation for $a$ with a final condition, and what remains is the integral against $\partial f/\partial\theta$. The multiplier is the sensitivity of the loss to the state at each time.

understand.title: Hard: memory against cost against stability
understand.text: Backpropagating through a solver with $N$ steps stores $N$ sets of intermediate values. The adjoint stores only the current state and recomputes $y(t)$ backwards, so memory does not depend on $N$, at the price of extra solver work and a gradient that matches the discrete one only up to solver error. If the forward ODE contracts, the backward recomputation of $y$ expands, and tiny errors grow: the continuous adjoint may give a poor gradient, and storing checkpoints of $y$ and re-integrating short segments between them fixes it.

understand.title: Hardest: the check can mislead if the step is wrong
understand.text: A central difference with a step that is too large has a large truncation error, and with a step near machine precision rounding dominates; both make a correct gradient look wrong. Sweep the step and look for a plateau where the relative error is smallest. If no step gives agreement better than the solver's own tolerance, the gradient or the loss is noisy, for instance because an adaptive solver changes its step with the weights; fix the solver steps or tighten the tolerances for the check.

steps.title: The problem
steps.note: Atlas S13 example 1 draws a descent along a gradient on a surface: the gradient with respect to the weights is what this page computes.

steps.title: Adjoint equation and gradient
steps.tex: \dot a=-\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\Big)^{\top}a,\quad a(T)=\Big(\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y}\Big)^{\top}\!\!\Big|_{y(T)},\qquad \frac{dL}{d\theta}=\int_0^T a^{\top}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\,dt
steps.note: Derived from the Lagrangian above. Integrate $y$, $a$ and the integral together from $T$ down to $0$.

steps.title: A case with a closed form
steps.note: For $\theta=1.5$, $T=2$ and $y^\ast=0.1$ the exact gradient is $+0.0049999093$ (computed).

steps.title: The adjoint of that problem
steps.note: Here $\partial f/\partial y=-\theta$ so the backward equation has the opposite sign and a grows toward $T$; $\partial f/\partial\theta=-y$. Quadrature gives 0.0049999093, and integrating the augmented system $(y,a,\text{integral})$ backwards with SciPy at tight tolerances matched the closed form to $5\times10^{-13}$.

steps.title: Central difference and its error
steps.note: The two terms balance near $\eta\approx\epsilon_{\text{mach}}^{1/3}$. On this problem the relative error was $1.3\times10^{-2}$ at $\eta=0.1$, $1.3\times10^{-6}$ at $10^{-3}$, $1.3\times10^{-10}$ at $10^{-5}$ (the best), $6.7\times10^{-9}$ at $10^{-8}$, $1.7\times10^{-6}$ at $10^{-11}$ and $1.0\times10^{-3}$ at $10^{-13}$.

steps.title: Reading the sweep
steps.note: A V-shaped curve on a log-log plot with its minimum near $10^{-5}$ is what a correct gradient looks like. A curve that stays high everywhere says the gradient (or the loss) is wrong or noisy. One-sided differences are less accurate: at $\eta=10^{-5}$ the forward difference had relative error $8.5\times10^{-8}$ against $1.3\times10^{-10}$ for central.

steps.title: Memory against cost
steps.note: For $N=1000$ steps backpropagation keeps 1000 sets of stage values, the adjoint keeps one state plus the running integral. The price is a second solve and the risk of an unstable backward reconstruction of $y$. Checkpointing sits between the two.

worked.title: Verify the adjoint gradient of a one-parameter decay and pick the finite-difference step
worked.problem: For $\dot y=-\theta y$, $y(0)=1$, $T=2$, $\ell=\tfrac12(y(T)-0.1)^2$ at $\theta=1.5$, compute the exact gradient, the adjoint gradient, and the relative central-difference error for $\eta=10^{-1},10^{-3},10^{-5},10^{-8},10^{-11}$. Which $\eta$ would you use?

solution.text: Central-difference relative errors, one for each step.
Choose the step at the bottom of the V.

worked.answer: Exact and adjoint gradients agree at 0.0049999093. The central difference is best near $10^{-5}$ with a relative error of $1.3\times10^{-10}$, so a check at that step with a pass threshold of $10^{-6}$ is comfortably in range; $10^{-1}$ fails by truncation and $10^{-11}$ by rounding.

analyze.hint: Two error sources with opposite dependence on the step.

evaluate.hint: Random points, random directions, all parameter groups.

evaluate.hint: Short integrations, stiff systems, exactness against the discrete scheme.

create: Write a gradient-check routine that tests a random direction $v$: compare $g^{\top}v$ with a central difference of $L(\theta+\eta v)$, and sweep $\eta$.
Design a test that distinguishes solver noise from a wrong gradient.
Sketch a checkpointing scheme for $N=10^4$ steps that stores 100 states.

checks.q: What does the adjoint state $a(t)$ measure?
checks.hint: Think of a small push on the state at time t.
checks.answer: The derivative of the final loss with respect to the state at time $t$: how much the loss changes per unit change of the state at that instant.

checks.q: For $\dot y=-\theta y$ what are $\partial f/\partial y$ and $\partial f/\partial\theta$?
Why does the finite-difference error rise again for very small steps?
checks.hint: What happens to the difference of two nearly equal numbers?
checks.answer: The numerator $L(\theta+\eta)-L(\theta-\eta)$ becomes the difference of nearly equal floating-point numbers, so rounding error of size $\epsilon_{\text{mach}}|L|$ divided by $\eta$ takes over.

checks.q: A gradient check reports a relative error of 4e-2 at eta = 1e-1 only. Is the gradient wrong?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: at that step the truncation error alone is of order $10^{-2}$ in this kind of problem. Repeat with smaller steps; a correct gradient shows the error falling by about 100 for each factor of 10.

checks.q: How do you check a gradient with respect to 10,000 weights cheaply?
checks.hint: One direction at a time is too slow.
checks.answer: Use random directions: compare $g^{\top}v$ with the central difference of the loss along $v$ for a few random $v$ and a few steps, instead of every component.
